author: Carlos Martinez
title: Rudskogen Motorsenter iRacing Guide: Setup, Strategy, Braking Zones
description: Master Rudskogen's flat, fast layout with setup tuning tips, braking point references, and race strategy for oval and road course variants.

sections.p: Rudskogen Motorsenter sits in southern Norway and presents one of the most underrated tracks in iRacing. The oval is flat, wide, and deceptively technical. Even though it looks simple on the monitor, the combination of high-speed turns, subtle banking, and variable grip surfaces catches drivers who arrive with a sloppy setup or lazy throttle control. I've spent enough laps here on my MOZA R9 to know where the grip lives and where it doesn't.

The track demands a balance between front-end stability in the corners and enough rear compliance to keep the car planted during the acceleration zone. Most setups fail because drivers chase too much downforce or lock the rear suspension solid, which costs time in the mid-corner and on exit. This guide walks through the physics, the braking points I use, and the setup philosophy that keeps my rig competitive lap after lap.

Rudskogen's road course variant is the primary option in iRacing, though the oval configuration also appears in some series. The road layout loops approximately 2.1 km with fast sweeps in the north complex and tighter technical sections mid-track. The surface is smooth asphalt with consistent grip, but banking is minimal across most corners, so mid-corner balance matters more than luck.

Turn 1 leads downhill into a long-radius left hander that opens all the way to the exit. Most cars arrive at this corner still trail-braking, so the entry is where you seal the lap time. Turns 3 and 4 form a fast chicane that punishes imprecision. The north loop (turns 5 to 8) is flat and flowing, with exit grip that transfers straight into the tight infield section. This is where many drivers lose time trying too hard on corner entry when the real work happens at mid-corner and exit.

list: Turn 1: Long left hander, downhill entry, grippy mid-corner, forgiving exit
Turns 3 and 4: Fast left-right chicane, requires smooth steering and patience
North loop: Flat, high-speed sweeps, minimal margin for over-steering
Infield section: Technical low-speed corners, transitional surface demands good car balance

sections.p: Braking is abrupt at Rudskogen. Turn 1 is the only heavy stop; most other corners demand threshold or light trail-braking. On my MOZA CRP2 load-cell pedals, I feel how much pressure the setup can tolerate before locking the fronts, and adjusting brake balance (usually rear-biased by 1 to 2 percent from the default) helps the car rotate without unsettling the rear.

I brake for Turn 1 between the 100-meter and 75-meter boards, depending on fuel and tire temperature. In the first lap or two, cold tires mean later braking; by lap 4 or 5, the same braking point often feels too early. This is why a consistent throttle application mid-corner matters—it's the bridge between braking stability and exit drive that lets you extract pace from the car's natural balance rather than fighting it.

list: Turn 1: Brake at 100m board, trail-brake until 50m board, exit at 60 percent throttle
Turns 3/4: Light trail-braking through turn 3, roll to full throttle between 3 and 4
North loop entries (turns 5, 6, 7): Threshold or threshold-adjacent braking, modulate mid-corner
Infield technical section: Light braking, emphasis on steering smoothness over pedal input

sections.tip: Rudskogen punishes throttle blips. Downshifting smoothly and matching revs on entry keeps the car settled. If the rear kicks on downshift, your engine brake is too high or your throttle application is abrupt.

sections.p: The setup I arrive with at Rudskogen is not a baseline to defend; it's a starting point I adjust within 10 to 15 minutes. The flat layout means front wing angle (usually ~3 to 5 degrees) is less critical than suspension stiffness. I start with a soft to moderate front anti-roll bar (~6 to 8 kN/m on most GT3 cars) to encourage mid-corner grip, then stiffen the rear slightly (~8 to 10 kN/m) to keep the platform stable on acceleration.

Brake balance sits around 54 to 56 percent rear for most entries. The small amount of rear bias prevents brake dive from pitching the nose down too much on turn-in at lower speeds, and it helps the rear stay planted during the longer deceleration zones. Ride height should keep the car level during corners; I watch for chassis roll in the slow-motion replay and dial brake pressure and roll stiffness in parallel.

Tire pressures are sensitive. Cold pressures around 24.5 to 25.0 psi front and 25.5 to 26.0 psi rear work as a starting point. In a longer race or hot track conditions, these climb to 25.5 to 26.0 front and 27.0 to 27.5 rear. Too soft and you run out of grip mid-corner. Too hard and the tire won't load properly on exit, which feels like a loss of mid-range consistency rather than a sudden snap.

list: Anti-roll bars: Soft front (6-8 kN/m), moderate rear (8-10 kN/m) for mid-corner grip and exit stability
Brake balance: 54-56% rear, adjusted if the car slides on turn-in or oversteers on exit
Ride height: Level or slightly nose-high to manage brake dive and maintain corner balance
Tire pressures: Begin 24.5-25.0 front / 25.5-26.0 rear, adjust in 0.3-0.5 increments per session

sections.p: Qualifying at Rudskogen rewards a single clean lap in a low-traffic window. I spend the first 5 laps warming tires and nailing the braking point into turn 1, then one all-out push lap, then a cool-down lap to preserve tire life if the qualifying session is long. The field typically spreads thin on this track—passing is possible but passing cleanly demands patience.

In a race, the opening lap sets the tone. Good pace into turn 1 and smooth mid-corner balance through the infield section separate the top third from the mid-field. I pay attention to tire degradation after lap 8 to 10; if the car is sliding earlier and requiring higher brake input, it's time to manage pressure and tire temperature rather than chase the leader. Tire management strategy at Rudskogen is about consistency, not aggression.

The north loop is a passing point, but only if your car is balanced. Trying to out-brake someone on the entry into turn 5 ends in a spinout if the track is slippery or if your setup is loose. I look for opportunities on the exit of turn 8 into the infield, where a tighter line or later throttle application can create a gap on the car ahead. Patience and smoothness win the race, not heroics.

sections.tip: Cold-tire lap one: prioritize turn-in stability and mid-corner grip over exit drive. Hot tires in lap two reward smoother throttle inputs. Don't rush the pace curve; let the track come to you.

sections.h2: Common mistakes and how to avoid them

sections.p: The most common error I see in Rudskogen races is over-aggressive turn-in. The flat surface and modest banking make the car feel like it has more grip than it does. Drivers arrive at turn 1 or the technical infield section with steering angle and throttle application locked in, then the rear slides and a spin follows. Smooth steering input and patience mid-corner—allowing the tire to load before asking for acceleration—eliminates half of the accidents on this track.

The second mistake is under-braking. Drivers arrive too fast, lock a wheel, and lose confidence in the braking system. I set my brake pressure around 95 to 100 percent and trust the setup. If you're locking, the problem is usually brake balance bias, not missing brake pressure. A rear-bias adjustment of 1 to 2 percent often restores confidence and lap time.

The third is chasing too much downforce. Rudskogen rewards a neutral, responsive car over a heavy one. If your setup feels sluggish on turn-in, reduce wing angle by 0.5 degrees and stiffen the front anti-roll bar by 0.5 kN/m before you add more brake pressure or brake bias. The car will feel more direct, and you'll naturally find a better pace.

list: Over-steering on entry: Smooth your steering input, allow the tire to load before mid-corner acceleration
Locking under braking: Adjust brake balance rear-bias by 1-2%, avoid excessive brake pressure
Heavy, sluggish turn-in: Reduce wing angle, stiffen front anti-roll bar, trust the tires

sections.p: Rudskogen is flat and smooth, which means your wheelbase and pedals matter more than your seating position or cockpit frame. My MOZA R9 direct-drive wheelbase communicates the grip threshold with enough detail that I can adjust throttle input 5 to 10 percent based on front-tire feedback alone. The load-cell brake pedal delivers this same precision on the brake input side. If you're running a belt-drive or gear-drive wheelbase, you're missing the micro-feedback that separates a 1:48 lap from a 1:47.

For pedals, a load-cell brake is essential. Rudskogen's braking demands modulation at low speeds and confidence at high speeds. A potentiometer-based brake pedal will have a dead zone or require too much travel to hit target brake pressure. On my MOZA CRP2 pedals, I can modulate brake input within millimeters of travel, which is the reason I can trail-brake consistently into turn 1.

Monitor setup is secondary but useful. A high refresh-rate display (120 Hz or higher) reveals the car's rotation earlier, which helps with mid-corner steering input and throttle timing. I use a 1440p 120 Hz display and notice the difference in my throttle application on exits; the earlier feedback means I can commit to full throttle earlier without guessing.

faqs.q: What is the ideal brake balance for Rudskogen, and how do I adjust it if the car is sliding on turn-in?
faqs.a: Start at 54-56% rear bias. If the car dives too much on turn-in or the rear slides, add 1-2% rear bias (so move to 55-58% rear). If the front locks under braking, reduce rear bias by 1-2%. Always adjust in small increments and test over three clean laps before making another change. Remember that tire temperature and fuel load also affect how the car behaves under braking.

faqs.q: How much should I adjust tire pressure between practice and a race at Rudskogen?
faqs.a: In practice, begin at 24.5-25.0 psi front and 25.5-26.0 psi rear cold. As the track heats up or the session continues, tires climb naturally. In a race with longer stints, expect pressures to rise to 25.5-26.0 front and 27.0-27.5 rear by midway through. Start conservatively and adjust in 0.3-0.5 psi steps if the car feels unstable mid-corner or understeer-prone on exit. Don't chase perfect pressures every lap; consistency matters more than precision.

faqs.q: What is the best approach to passing at Rudskogen, and where are the overtaking points?
faqs.a: Passing is safest on exit from the north loop (exit of turn 8) into the infield straight, where a tighter line and smooth throttle application can build an advantage. The entry into turn 1 is also a passing point, but only if you arrive with a composed car and your opponent is loose or vulnerable. Avoid aggressive dive-bomb attempts into the technical infield corners; the risk of contact is high and the pass probability is low. Patience and smooth driving separate good racers from frustrated ones at this track.

faqs.q: My car feels sluggish and unresponsive on turn-in. Should I add more brake pressure or adjust wing angle first?
faqs.a: Adjust wing angle first. Reduce front wing by 0.5 degrees and see if the car feels more direct over three laps. If it does, you've found the issue. If the car still feels heavy, then adjust the front anti-roll bar up by 0.5 kN/m. Brake pressure is a last resort; often the problem is aerodynamic balance or suspension stiffness, not braking capability. Making one small adjustment per session keeps your data clean and helps you learn what the car actually needs.
